\begin{abstract}
This project fits a multiple linear regression for the response against the remaining covariates, diagnoses extreme multicollinearity, and applies elastic-net regularization with glmnet over a grid of alpha values. The best model is chosen by cross-validation using the one-standard-error rule.
\end{abstract}

# DATA EXTRACTION AND PREPROCESSING
```{r}
load("data/raw/AEM_03_Regularization_data.RData")
```

# DATA SET PREPARATION 
Removal of 6 variables according to the ID number. If the ID ends in “abcd”, remove 6 variables among  
x1a,  x2a,  x3a,  x1b,  x2b,  x4b,  x1c,  x3c,  x4c,  x2d,   x3d,   x4d  
```{r}
a=9 
b=3
c=5
d=6 
elim=c(19,29,39,13,23,43) 
datos=datos[,-elim] 
```

# MULTIPLE LINEAR MODEL  
Obtain the multiple regression model of variable Yj against the remaining variables. Analyse the 
multicollinearity problem.

## MODEL CONSTRUCTION
```{r}
lm.fit <- lm(Y~.,data=datos)
summary(lm.fit)
```
We observe that the model should exclude several variables that are not statistically significant. Even so, it achieves a good $R^2$. We also find a low $p$-value, rejecting the fundamental hypothesis test, i.e., rejecting that all model coefficients are equal to $0$.

## RESIDUAL ANALYSIS
```{r}
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(lm.fit)
```
The residuals appear consistent with normality.

## MULTICOLLINEARITY ANALYSIS
```{r}
vif(lm.fit) 
```
There is extreme multicollinearity, which indicates that this model cannot be implemented because it fails the assumptions. Recall that values above 5 are considered evidence of multicollinearity, and here the VIFs are highly disproportionate. 

```{r}
det(vcov(lm.fit))
```
The determinant of the design covariance matrix is extremely small, which would make the linear model “blow up”.


# REGULARIZATION MODEL
Apply elastic-net regularization with the glmnet library for alpha values: 0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95, 1. Choose the best model by cross-validation and compare the models obtained.

## MODEL CONSTRUCTION
We prepare the design matrix and the response vector.
```{r}
mx=as.matrix(datos[,2:ncol(datos)])  
my=as.matrix(datos[,1])
```

We build cross-validated models over 12 $\alpha$ values and the default 100 $\lambda$ values, for up to 1200 models as an upper bound. 
```{r}
alphas <- c(0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95, 1)

cv_models <- lapply(alphas, function(a) {
  set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
  cv.glmnet(mx,my,keep=TRUE, alpha = a)
})
```

## MODEL SELECTION
We use the $1se$ rule to select the best model for each $alpha$.
```{r}
cv_1se <- function(cv_models, alphas){
cv_errors_1se <- sapply(cv_models, function(model) {
  model$cvm[which(model$lambda == model$lambda.1se)]
})
cv_lambda_index <- sapply(cv_models, function(model) {
  which(model$lambda == model$lambda.1se)
})
cv_lambda_value <- sapply(cv_models, function(model) {
  model$lambda[which(model$lambda == model$lambda.1se)]
})

df<- data.frame(
  cvm = cv_errors_1se,
  lambda_index = cv_lambda_index,
  lambda = cv_lambda_value,
  alphas = alphas
)
return(df)
}
df=cv_1se(cv_models,alphas)
df
```
Note that the CVM is very similar across all $\alpha$ values.

We now check which $\alpha$ yields the best results in terms of mean squared error.
```{r}
best_alpha_model_index <-which(df$cvm == min(df$cvm))
best_alpha_model_params <- df[best_alpha_model_index,]
best_alpha_model_params
```
The best model has $\alpha=0.45$.

```{r}
set.seed(123)
best_alpha_model = cv.glmnet(mx,my,keep=TRUE, alpha = 0.45)
```

We now inspect some features of the best model.  
We find a suitable value for $\lambda$.
```{r}
nCVopt = which(best_alpha_model$lambda == best_alpha_model$lambda.1se)
best_alpha_model$lambda[nCVopt]
```

We plot the information about $\lambda$.
```{r}
plot(best_alpha_model)
```


```{r}
best_alpha_model$glmnet.fit
```

```{r}
coef(best_alpha_model)
```
Although $\lambda = 0.02876513$ is optimal under the 1se rule, a larger $\lambda$ may be preferable here; for example, $0.0729$ still keeps an $R^2$ of about $93\%$ but with 27 variables instead of 34.

Finally, we make a prediction with the 1se model. 

```{r}
mxpred=mx[1001:1010,]  
predict(best_alpha_model, mxpred,   s = best_alpha_model$lambda.1se, type=c("link")) 
```
